facts.fact_text: On 20 June 1997 the public authorities prevented the applicant and her daughter from attending a meeting organised by a radio station in southern Cyprus, by not giving them permission to cross over to the southern part of Cyprus.
On the anniversary of Kutlu Adalı's death the applicant organised a ceremony to commemorate her husband.
The day before the meeting in southern Cyprus, the applicant received a phone call from an official in the "TRNC Ministry of Foreign Affairs".
Being scared by the phone call from the "TRNC Ministry of Foreign Affairs" official, the applicant decided not to attend the meeting in southern Cyprus.
Plain-clothes policemen have constantly been following the applicant and her daughter.
The applicant's and her daughter's phones had been tapped and their correspondence monitored.
The applicant and her daughter received anonymous phone calls.
The applicant's telephone and fax line has been disconnected from time to time.
The applicant maintains that the water supply of her house has been cut on several occasions and she does not believe that this was due to technical faults as alleged by the Council Water Department.

The "TRNC" regime refused to register an association called the "Kutlu Adalı Foundation", whose aims include the furthering of the ideas of Kutlu Adalı regarding peace, democracy, human rights and freedom.
The applicant's request to keep her husband's press card was rejected.

On 20 June 1997 the public authorities prevented the applicant and her daughter from attending a meeting organised by a radio station in southern Cyprus, by not giving them permission to cross over to the southern part of Cyprus.
On the day of the commemoration ceremony for Kutlu Adalı, the municipality brought in digging machines to dig up the road just under the applicant's street.
A picture of Kutlu Adalı, which was displayed in the applicant's garden, was stolen.
On 10 August 1997 the applicant heard three gunshots outside her home.
Before the applicant left for England, a real-estate agent came to meet her daughter and told her to sell their house and accept any offer he would make to buy it.
The applicant believes that the real-estate agent was sent by the "TRNC" authorities to persuade her to leave the country.
The applicant contends that following her application to the European Court of Human Rights, her daughter was dismissed from her post in a bank.
The applicant contends that although her daughter was ranked 15th among 68 candidates in the examination to become a civil servant, she was not given a post.
According to the applicant's representatives, Professor Bakır Çağlar allegedly told the applicant that she might be assassinated if she won her case before the Court.
According to the applicant's representatives, Professor Bakır Çağlar allegedly told the applicant that her daughter's scholarship would be discontinued.
On 15 October 1996 the applicant submitted a petition to the Telephone Directorate in Nicosia, stating that she and her family had been disturbed by calls made from a certain number.
At the applicant's request, a tapping device was put on to the applicant's telephone line (no. 2274089).
On 12 November 1996 a call was received from telephone number 2271851, and the authorities found out that the number belonged to a certain Mr Cahit Hüray, whose telephone line was then cut off.

On 22 November 1996, an assistant police inspector took statements from the head of the technical section at the Telephone Directorate to clarify the matter of the call from Mr Cahit Hüray's telephone number to the applicant.
The Government note that the applicant herself asked for protection from the "TRNC" authorities and was told that she was already under the protection of plain-clothes policemen.
The Government submit that in order to register a foundation in the name of Kutlu Adalı, an application should be made to the competent court and a court order should be obtained.
On 2 April 1998 the Nicosia Family Court ordered the registration of the Kutlu Adalı Foundation after the applicant and eight other persons followed the correct procedure.

The Government submit that crossings of the Green Line to and from the Ledra Palace Gate between the "TRNC" and southern Cyprus are regulated by the rules and regulations of the "TRNC" and are subject to restrictions due to security precautions.
The Government submit that the "TRNC" authorities have the right to suspend permission to cross the border at the Ledra Palace Gate.
The applicant had been subjected to constant harassment after the death of her husband, including receiving threatening telephone calls.
When the applicant informed the police about threatening telephone calls in 1996, they managed to trace a call to one Cahit Hüray who lived two streets away.
Mr Cahit Hüray was let off after paying a miserly fine, and the threatening telephone calls continued.

The applicant received a telephone call from a man calling himself Ali who said that he was coming over to determine her fate; she informed the police as the indicator had shown the number that had been used, but the police did nothing.

One evening, as the applicant was returning home after a meeting and stopped off at a neighbour's, she was told that there was somebody walking around in her garden; it turned out to be a neighbour who was near the water tank and did not explain what he was doing there.
The next day after the water tank incident, the applicant found that her dog was dead, with its ribs and one of its legs broken.

The veterinary surgeon who conducted the autopsy on the applicant's dog said that the dog had not been run over by a car, because of a lack of tyre marks on the place where it was found, and that the dog had been severely tortured elsewhere and then taken to the applicant's garden.
The applicant's water and electricity were regularly cut off.
Mail addressed to the applicant was either not delivered or was opened.
The applicant's telephone calls were monitored.
The applicant's complaints to the police, both orally and in writing, about the harassment she experienced led to nothing.
The application to establish the Adalı Foundation, which sixty democratic organisations wanted to set up in order to continue Kutlu Adalı's work, was initially refused.
The registration fee for the Adalı Foundation was increased fivefold and the applicant sold a plot of land to raise the money.
The charter of the Adalı Foundation had to be changed; for example, the phrase "democratic activities" was replaced by "cultural activities".
In July 1996, the applicant's daughter was told she would get a job in the public sector but this did not materialise.
The applicant's daughter found a job in a bank, but her contract of employment was terminated from one day to the next, allegedly for disciplinary reasons.
The applicant contends that her daughter's dismissal from the bank was in reality because the applicant had lodged an application with the Court.
The applicant's daughter's scholarship had recently been discontinued at the time of the applicant's oral evidence.
Tansel told the applicant that unless she withdrew her application to the European Court of Human Rights she would be arrested.

The applicant and her husband received various threats intended to deter Mr Kutlu Adalı from continuing to express his opinions.
Between January 1980 and July 1996, unknown persons subjected Mr Kutlu Adalı to various forms of harassment.
Mr Kutlu Adalı's house was attacked with machine guns.
Mr Kutlu Adalı received frequent threatening phone calls.
After the publication of the article about the St Barnabas monastery theft, the editor of the Yenidüzen newspaper received a threatening phone call from the head of the Civil Defence Organisation.
After the publication of the article about the St Barnabas monastery theft, Mr Kutlu Adalı began to receive frequent threatening phone calls.
On 6 July 1996, at around 11.35 p.m., the applicant's husband, Mr Kutlu Adalı, was shot and killed in front of his house in the "TRNC" by unknown persons.
The applicant attempted to investigate her husband's death herself.
The applicant learned from her neighbours that within only a few minutes of the shooting about twelve military cars had arrived and had sealed off the area.
The applicant learned from her neighbours that the "special teams" of police officers had threatened the neighbours with guns to force them to go back inside their houses.

Three days after Mr Kutlu Adalı was killed, the applicant's family received a telephone call from an anonymous female caller who gave the names of two individuals she said were responsible for Mr Kutlu Adalı's murder: a Mr Hüseyin Demirci and a man whose first name was Orhan.
The applicant informed the police about the anonymous phone call naming Mr Hüseyin Demirci and a man named Orhan as responsible for Mr Kutlu Adalı's murder.
The police refused to start an investigation based on the anonymous phone call, stating that the woman caller was known for making false allegations to the police.
On 14 July 1996 the applicant's children arranged a meeting with the President of the "TRNC".
At the meeting on 14 July 1996, the applicant's children requested the President of the "TRNC" to take steps to ensure that effective action was taken to find their father's killer.
At the meeting on 14 July 1996, the President of the "TRNC" promised to take effective action to find Mr Kutlu Adalı's killer.
In December 1996 the applicant went to see the security forces' commander, Mr Hasan Peker Günal, and complained that the security forces were not investigating her husband's death properly.

On 5 March 1997 the Yenidüzen newspaper published a letter signed by the head of the "Grey Wolves", which contained a threat that left-wing journalists and writers would be killed like Mr Kutlu Adalı.
The applicant gave copies of the article containing the threat from the head of the "Grey Wolves" to the police to investigate, but she did not receive any response.

On 26 June 1997 the applicant wrote to the security forces' commander, Mr Hasan Peker Günal, pointing out that nearly one year had passed since her husband's assassination and that the perpetrators had not yet been found.
The applicant did not receive any concrete information in reply to her letter of 26 June 1997 to the security forces' commander, Mr Hasan Peker Günal.

The Government submit that on 6 July 1996 at 11.40 p.m. a tip-off was received at the communications section of the Lefkoşa Police Headquarters on telephone no. 155 from an unidentified caller, stating that there had been a murder at the point where Ardıç Street crosses Akasya Street.

Following the tip-off, two Land Rovers belonging to the special unit (çevik birlik) of the nearby Yenişehir police station, attached to the Lefkoşa Police Headquarters, came to the scene of the incident within a short time.
The Land Rovers from the Yenişehir police station were followed by police vehicles bringing Criminal Investigation Department personnel from the Yenişehir and Lefkoşa Police Stations.
The immediate area of the incident and the surrounding area were cordoned off by police officers who started to work in order to identify the culprits.
Early in the morning of 7 July 1996, at 3 a.m., police officers brought a doctor from the Nicosia (Lefkoşa) State Hospital to the scene of the incident.
The doctor who examined Mr Kutlu Adalı's body established that Mr Adalı had died at the scene of the incident as a result of two bullet wounds in the areas of his left temple and left shoulder.
A photographic fingerprinting officer took photographs of the scene of the incident where Mr Kutlu Adalı was killed.
A sketch map of the scene of the incident indicated the positions of the empty cartridges found at the scene of Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing.
Mr Kutlu Adalı's body was sent to the Nicosia State Hospital morgue for the purposes of an autopsy.
On 7 July 1996 police officers drew up a list of residents, including the applicant's neighbours, in the Akasya and Ardıç streets.
On 7 July 1996 statements were taken from thirty-three persons as to their knowledge about the incident of Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing.

Following the autopsy carried out by Dr İsmail Bundak on 7 July 1996, the cause of Mr Kutlu Adalı's death was identified as dismemberment of the internal organs, internal haemorrhage and subdural bleeding at the head as a result of the wounds sustained by being shot with a firearm.

Between 8 and 31 July 1996 twenty-six further statements were taken from potential witnesses, including members of the applicant's family, in connection with the investigation into Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing.
The authorities investigated the applicant's allegations that at the time her husband was killed the street lights at the scene of the incident and in the vicinity were switched off.

Subsequent to enquiries made by Mr Ali Horoz, an equipment engineer at the Turkish Cyprus Electricity Company, it was established that the electricity for the street lights at the place of the incident and in the nearby Akasya, Akalan, Bağarası, Söğüt and Altınova Streets was provided by the "Sıdıka Çatozlu" power supply and not from the power supply of the Civil Defence Organisation as alleged by the applicant.
After statements had been taken from residents in the area, it was established that there had not been a power cut on the night of Mr Kutlu Adalı's murder.

It was further established that even if the power supply in the courtyard of the Civil Defence Headquarters had been interfered with, it would not have been possible to switch off the street lights at the scene of the incident or in the streets in the vicinity.
A ballistic examination was carried out on 14 used cartridges found at the scene of Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing.
The ballistics report of 6 August 1996 stated that the 14 used cartridges were 9-mm Parabellum-type cartridges that had been fired from one single gun at close range.

The ballistics report of 6 August 1996 noted that the cartridges and the bullet cores were not linked to any other cartridges or bullet cores that had hitherto been found within the territory of the "TRNC" or recorded in the files on murders by unknown assailants.
On 4 March 1998 the police assistant inspector in charge of the investigation into Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing, Ahmet Soyalan, concluded his report on the investigation.

In his concluding remarks, police assistant inspector Ahmet Soyalan stated that it had not been possible to identify the murderer(s) of Mr Kutlu Adalı and that he could not therefore reach a positive result for the investigation.
On 29 April 1998 the case of Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing was referred to the Attorney-General of the "TRNC".
On 1 July 1998 the Attorney-General's office advised that the matter of Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing should be referred to a coroner for an inquest.
On 31 July 1998 the Nicosia Police Chief informed the Nicosia Coroner of the results of the investigation into the killing of Mr Kutlu Adalı.
The Nicosia Police Chief transmitted to the Nicosia Coroner the full investigation file containing the statements of the witnesses and the investigating officer's report.
The hearing before the coroner in Lefkoşa commenced on 20 October 1998.
Following statements from witnesses, the coroner's hearing was concluded on 11 December 1998 with the delivery of the verdict.

The coroner found that Kutlu Adalı had been shot dead on 6 July 1996 by unidentified person(s), and that his death had been caused by organ dismemberment, internal haemorrhage and subdural haemorrhage in the head.
The coroner stated that the murderer(s) of Kutlu Adalı could not be identified and declared the case closed.

Public statements were made by the President, the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly, the Prime Minister and political party leaders of the "TRNC", condemning the killing of Mr Kutlu Adalı and calling for the assailants to be found.
The facts of the case being in dispute between the parties, the Court conducted an investigation with the assistance of the parties.
Four delegates of the Court took oral evidence from the applicant on 8 October 2002.
Six further witnesses were heard by the Court's Delegates on 23 and 24 June 2003 in Lefkoşa, Cyprus.

On the day of publication of the St Barnabas article on 17 March 1996, the head of the Civil Defence Organisation, Galip Mendi, telephoned the Yenidüzen newspaper and made threats, which were indirectly aimed at Mr Kutlu Adalı because he was the author of the article.
Mr Kutlu Adalı received many anonymous letters saying that he would be killed in a week's time, and threatening telephone calls.
As Mr Kutlu Adalı was a very proud person, he did not report the threats to the police, although he did mention them in an article of 23 April 1996.
Mr Kutlu Adalı did not try to have the threatening telephone calls traced.

Being of the firm belief that her husband had been assassinated by Government agents, the applicant herself conducted an investigation and handed the results, in the form of a written statement, to the police chief Mehmet Özdamar.
None of the inhabitants of Şehit Ecvet Yusuf Street were interviewed by the police in connection with Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing.
The police said that the inhabitants of Şehit Ecvet Yusuf Street had not been at home when the incident had occurred, but the applicant stated this was not true.
Two neighbours who were Turkish students living in the basement of the building next door refused to speak to the applicant and left Cyprus three days after the killing of Mr Kutlu Adalı.
The two Turkish student neighbours did give a statement to the police.
Erinç Aydınova had made a statement to the police, but it was not complete: the boy did not tell the police that he had seen a car passing at great speed.

Feri Khan and her mother lived across from the applicant's house, were at home on the night of the murder, saw a black Murat car without licence plates and heard shots, but the police had never asked them for statements.
According to the police, Feri Khan and her mother had not been at home on the night of Mr Kutlu Adalı's murder.
The applicant believed that Mr Ziya Kasaboğlu was involved in the incident because he did not come to speak to her and the police did not take a statement from him.

The applicant asked the authorities to take a statement from Mr Ziya Kasaboğlu, but to no avail, first making this request at a secret meeting in December 1996 with Hasan Peker Günal, commander of the security forces, and Attila Sav, the chief of police, which took place in the latter's office.
On the first night when the applicant was questioned, police chief Mehmet Özdamar told her that Altay Sayıl was a good person and insinuated that Mr Sayıl had nothing to do with the murder.
Altay Sayıl did not come to the applicant's house for ten days after the murder; and then he only came because the applicant asked him to.

Shortly after Mr Kutlu Adalı had been killed, a large number of police officers went into the applicant's house, ostensibly to guarantee the security of the house because, according to them, they found the door open and the television switched on.
The police officers who entered the applicant's house turned everything upside down and it took the applicant and her family two years to restore order amongst her husband's books and papers.
The muhtar Tahsin Ali Rıza was never questioned by the police.
The police never took a statement from Orhan Ceylan, although Mr Hüseyin Demirci was interviewed by them.
A statement was not taken from Mustafa Asilhan, who had dinner with Mr Hüseyin Demirci on the evening of the murder according to the latter's statement.
When Mr Hüseyin Demirci was taken to hospital by local people after his car was shot at, he shouted that an attempt had been made to kill him because he had killed Kutlu Adalı.
The local people who heard Mr Hüseyin Demirci's statement at the hospital informed the police, but were told to forget about it.
Following the murder, the applicant spoke to Dr İsmail Bundak, who told her that no post mortem had been carried out but that her husband's body had been X-rayed.

The applicant was unable to find out whether a post mortem had been carried out until, after she had lodged her application with the former Commission, she obtained a copy of the post mortem report together with the Government's observations.
In 1997 the applicant had a meeting with Fikri Sağlar, a member of the Turkish Parliament and chairman of the Turkish Susurluk committee.
In 1998 and in 2001 the Parliament of the "TRNC" established its own Susurluk investigation committee, suspecting that there was a connection between Abdullah Çatlı and the murder of Kutlu Adalı.
The applicant made statements to the "TRNC" Susurluk investigation committees but did not have transcripts of her statements.

The "TRNC" Susurluk investigation committees came to the conclusion that Abdullah Çatlı had visited Cyprus, using false identities, on many occasions and that around the time of Mr Kutlu Adalı's murder he had been staying at the Jasmine Court hotel, with his expenses being paid by the army.

Although the roads in the vicinity of the applicant's house were very quickly closed off by the military after the shooting of her husband, the roads in the outlying area, and especially those leading to the airport, were not.
A taxi driver told the applicant that he had taken Abdullah Çatlı to the airport directly after the murder of Mr Kutlu Adalı had been committed.
At the secret meeting with Hasan Peker Günal and Attila Sav in December 1996, the applicant informed them of her suspicions about Altay Sayıl, Ziya Kasaboğlu, Hüseyin Demirci and Abdullah Çatlı.
At the December 1996 meeting, Hasan Peker Günal said that he had never heard the name of Altay Sayıl before but that he would follow it up.
The applicant was of the opinion that the security forces were opposed to an effective investigation being carried out into the killing of her husband.

Shortly after the killing of Mr Kutlu Adalı, Refik Öztümen, who was in charge of the judicial investigation, wanted to meet with the applicant at her sister-in-law's house, but the applicant refused because she was afraid at that time.

Refik Öztümen told the applicant's sister-in-law that he had been given instructions by the security forces not to conduct the investigation effectively and that the applicant should not follow it up either.
When the applicant informed the police about threatening telephone calls in 1996, they managed to trace a call to one Cahit Hüray who lived two streets away.
Mr Cahit Hüray was let off after paying a miserly fine, and the threatening telephone calls continued.

The applicant received a telephone call from a man calling himself Ali who said that he was coming over to determine her fate; she informed the police as the indicator had shown the number that had been used, but the police did nothing.
The applicant's complaints to the police, both orally and in writing, about the harassment she experienced led to nothing.
Ahmet Soyalan was responsible for the investigation into the killing of Kutlu Adalı.
Ahmet Soyalan started his investigation into the killing of Kutlu Adalı at 9 a.m. on 7 July 1996.

Although it was possible that Mr Kutlu Adalı had been killed because of his activities as a journalist, Ahmet Soyalan also looked into Mr Adalı's personal life and his personality as part of the investigation.
Ahmet Soyalan was only informed of the murder of Mr Kutlu Adalı the following morning and received a short briefing from Mr Refik Öztümen as to what had been done the previous night.

Ahmet Soyalan did not consider it necessary to take a statement from Chief Inspector Eybil Efendi initially because he had been briefed by Mr Refik Öztümen, who had arrived at the scene so soon after Mr Efendi that the latter would not have seen anything different.

In 2002, Ahmet Soyalan took a statement from Chief Inspector Eybil Efendi in order to show that, contrary to what the applicant alleged, no military vehicles were present at the scene and that the vehicles of the rapid response unit resembled military vehicles.

Ahmet Soyalan was told by Mr Refik Öztümen that after the discovery of Mr Kutlu Adalı's body, police had entered the applicant's house, together with the muhtar, in order to check if any of the family members were at home and if they were safe, and also to see if any clues about the murder could be found there.
Nothing untoward was found in the applicant's house; no search as such was carried out, merely a visual inspection.
It was not considered necessary to take a statement from the muhtar, as no evidence was found in the house and nothing untoward happened.
No fingerprint examination was carried out at the applicant's house, given that the incident had taken place outside the house and the interior of the house was thus not a crime scene.

From the statements taken by Mr Refik Öztümen and his colleagues directly after the incident, it appeared that a dark-coloured car with many lights at the rear had been seen near the scene of Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing.
A search was carried out on the night of Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing but the vehicle, which had left the scene at high speed, was not found.

Ahmet Soyalan started his investigation on the morning after the incident by taking statements from the people living in the area of the scene of the crime, with this work having already commenced the previous evening.
Statements were taken from all persons who had been at home at the time of the incident, regardless of whether or not they had any information to offer.
It was the local police officers, who knew the area and its inhabitants well, who established who had been at home and who had not on the night of Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing.
Since no statement was taken from Feri Khan and her mother, Ahmet Soyalan concluded they must have been out when the offence had taken place.
Ahmet Soyalan took the applicant's statement on the evening of 7 July 1996, after she had returned from Turkey.

The applicant expressed to Ahmet Soyalan her opinion that the killing of her husband was connected to the articles he had written about the St Barnabas incident and that the head of the Civil Defence Organisation, Mr Galip Mendi, had been annoyed by these articles and had telephoned Yenidüzen making threats against her husband.

The applicant persistently claimed to Ahmet Soyalan that the murder had been arranged by the administration of the Civil Defence Organisation and that she held the head of that organisation responsible.

Not even the smallest piece of evidence could be found to support the allegation that the Civil Defence Organisation was involved in Mr Kutlu Adalı's murder, and for that reason no statements were taken from the head or other persons belonging to the Civil Defence Organisation.
A statement could not be taken from Mr Galip Mendi because he had gone abroad; Mr Mendi returned in 2001 as the commander of the security forces.
The applicant alleged that on the night of the murder the street lighting in Ardıç Street, where she lived, had been switched off at the transformer substation in the Civil Defence Organisation.
The matter of the street lighting was examined and it was established through the taking of statements that the street lights had been on on the night of Mr Kutlu Adalı's murder.
It was further established that power for the lighting in Ardıç Street was supplied from a different substation than the one in the Civil Defence Organisation.
In her statement to Ahmet Soyalan, the applicant mentioned Ahmet Cavit An, according to whom Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing was a politically motivated murder.

Ahmet Soyalan went to see Ahmet Cavit An, once at his house and once at the clinic where he worked, but Mr Cavit An was unable to provide any useful information as to the secret cells allegedly involved in the murder.
In order to obtain a copy of documents such as the post mortem and ballistic reports, permission from the Attorney-General's office was required.
Ahmet Soyalan took two statements from Altay Sayıl in connection with the investigation into Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing.
Ahmet Soyalan first interviewed Altay Sayıl because he had been informed that Mr Sayıl was a close friend of Mr Kutlu Adalı.
In the light of articles that subsequently appeared in newspapers, Ahmet Soyalan felt the need to take a more in-depth statement from Altay Sayıl.

The weapon used to kill Mr Kutlu Adalı could not be identified; a number of spent cartridges were found at the site from which it could be established that they had been fired by a 9 mm firearm, but the make of the weapon remained unknown.
Ballistic tests were carried out both in Turkey and in the "TRNC" to see if the bullets used to kill Mr Kutlu Adalı had been fired by a weapon known to the authorities, but to no avail.

The ballistic tests included comparisons of sample cartridges held in the archives of the "TRNC" of all the weapons registered in the names of persons in the "TRNC", such as the weapon belonging to Mr Orhan Ceylan.

Ahmet Soyalan assumed that the Turkish authorities had examined whether the spent cartridges had been fired by the Uzi found in the car in which Abdullah Çatlı had died in Susurluk in November 1996, but he had not been informed of any result.

The investigation showed that Abdullah Çatlı had not been in the "TRNC" at the time of Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing, as there were no records of him entering the "TRNC" at the relevant time under any of the identities which Mr Çatlı was known to have used.

The applicant did not inform Ahmet Soyalan or any other police officers that she had received an anonymous telephone call from a woman alleging that Mr Hüseyin Demirci and a man with the first name Orhan had been involved in the killing of Mr Kutlu Adalı.
Some time after the incident, a woman who could not be identified telephoned Mr Yusuf Özkum, the then head of the judicial branch, and gave him the name of Hüseyin Demirci.
Mr Yusuf Özkum passed the name of Hüseyin Demirci on to Mr Mehmet Özdamar, who proceeded to take Mr Demirci's statement.
On the evening of Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing, Mr Hüseyin Demirci had dinner with Mustafa Asilhan, the then assistant chief of police, in Gemikonağı.

Although no statement was taken from Mustafa Asilhan at the time, Mr Mehmet Özdamar spoke to Mr Asilhan about the matter, and Mr Asilhan said that Police Officer Muharrem Göç had seen the two men having dinner.
Police Officer Muharrem Göç subsequently confirmed in a statement to Mr Mehmet Özdamar that he had seen Mr Hüseyin Demirci and Mustafa Asilhan having dinner on the evening of 6 July 1996.
Mustafa Asilhan himself confirmed that he had had dinner with Mr Hüseyin Demirci on 6 July 1996 when his statement was taken in 2002.

Ahmet Soyalan did not consider it likely that Mr Hüseyin Demirci could have been involved in the killing of Mr Kutlu Adalı after he had left the restaurant because such an assassination required preparation.

Mr Hüseyin Demirci said that he had gone straight home after dropping off Mustafa Asilhan, and as Mr Mehmet Özdamar had not formed the opinion that Mr Demirci was speaking anything other than the truth, this matter was not examined further.

Ahmet Soyalan checked to see whether Mr Hüseyin Demirci had a criminal record as there was an allegation that he had been acquitted on a murder charge, but there was no information that he had ever committed any criminal offence.

Ahmet Soyalan examined whether Mr Hüseyin Demirci had been admitted to hospital with burns, as alleged by the applicant, and established that Mr Demirci had spent three days in hospital in February 1997 for broken ribs.
Mr Hüseyin Demirci was not asked about his hospital stay because it did not coincide with the murder of Mr Kutlu Adalı.

Ahmet Soyalan stated that had the incident alleged by the applicant really occurred — namely that Mr Hüseyin Demirci opened fire inside the hospital, saying "I killed Kutlu Adalı" — it would have been reported to the police.
The information reported to the police was only connected to Mr Hüseyin Demirci and did not mention Orhan Ceylan.
At some point there was a report in the press to the effect that Orhan Ceylan had committed the murder of Mr Kutlu Adalı along with Mr Hüseyin Demirci.

Orhan Ceylan's statement was not taken at the time of the initial investigation given that Mr Hüseyin Demirci's whereabouts on the evening of the murder had already been established and it was thus known that Mr Demirci had not been in contact with Mr Ceylan that night.

Ahmet Soyalan took a statement from Orhan Ceylan on 18 October 2002, only because his name had come up in the application to the Court, as there was not a shred of evidence or any indication that he had been involved in the killing.
Ahmet Soyalan took a statement from Ziya Kasapoğlu on 21 October 2002, because his name was mentioned in the application to the Court.

Prior to taking the statement on 21 October 2002, Ahmet Soyalan was not aware that Ziya Kasapoğlu might possess information relating to the incident, as Mr Kasapoğlu's shop was in Şehit Ecvet Yusuf Street, far from the scene of the crime.
Ahmet Soyalan was requested by the Agent of the respondent Government, Professor Necatigil, to carry out an investigation in connection with the allegations made by the applicant to the Court.
Ahmet Soyalan received no specific instructions from Professor Necatigil, only a document containing the applicant's allegations.
Mehmet Özdamar supervised the investigation into the killing of Mr Kutlu Adalı and was the supervisor of Ahmet Soyalan and Refik Öztümen.
Mehmet Özdamar was informed about the incident by the switchboard and arrived at the scene of the incident within ten or fifteen minutes.
The officers marked and numbered the empty cartridges and cordoned the area off with a view to preventing unauthorised persons from walking around the scene of Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing.
A sketch-map of the scene of Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing was drawn up and a team was set up in order to take testimonies from people nearby.
Mehmet Özdamar entered Mr Kutlu Adalı's house three or four hours after the incident, along with Refik Öztümen, a close relative of the deceased and the local muhtar.
Mehmet Özdamar and those with him looked for a document, an item or anything that could have been the cause of the incident but did not remove any object.
Mehmet Özdamar did not consider it necessary to look for fingerprints in the applicant's house since the incident had happened in the street and not in the house.

When investigating the murder of Mr Kutlu Adalı, every aspect of the case was considered, including whether it was a political crime or one related to Mr Adalı's activities as a journalist, but there was no evidence significant enough to lead to any of these conclusions.

Mehmet Özdamar was informed about the applicant's allegation that the head of the Civil Defence Organisation had made threats against Mr Kutlu Adalı personally or against the Yenidüzen newspaper because of an article concerning the St Barnabas incident.

The prosecuting authorities did not verify the allegation about the Civil Defence Organisation's head making threats since the applicant could not name anyone and she had constantly made similar inconsistent allegations.

Following the receipt of an anonymous telephone call alleging that a person named Hüseyin Demirci and another person described as Colonel Orhan were involved in the killing of Mr Kutlu Adalı, the prosecuting authorities found Mr Demirci and took statements from him.

It was established that Mr Hüseyin Demirci had been outside Lefkoşa on the night of Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing, having been at a dinner in the Güzelyurt area in the company of Mustafa Asilhan, who was the first assistant of the Chief of Police, and Muharrem Göç, a police inspector.
Mustafa Asilhan confirmed to Mehmet Özdamar that he had been out for dinner with Mr Hüseyin Demirci on the night of Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing.
A statement was also taken from Muharrem Göç confirming the dinner between Mr Hüseyin Demirci and Mustafa Asilhan.

Regarding a tip-off to Yusuf Özkum, who was then the Chief of Police, about Mr Hüseyin Demirci, Mehmet Özdamar stated that they had had no chance to investigate the woman caller since she had not given her name and had asked her identity to be kept secret.

No investigation was conducted into the Turkish Revenge Brigade's claim of responsibility as such an organisation did not exist in the "TRNC" and the investigating authorities considered that the allegation had been made as a ploy designed to cause confusion.
Documents contained in the investigation file were confidential; only the investigating officer and his superiors as well as the Attorney-General's office could have access to them.
Refik Öztümen was informed about the incident at 11.40 p.m. at the station and sent the sergeant on duty to the scene of the incident together with a team.
Refik Öztümen asked for a doctor from the local hospital to be sent to the scene of the incident.
Refik Öztümen went to the scene of the crime along with a police officer and arrived there at 11.45 p.m.
At around 3 or 3.30 a.m. Refik Öztümen entered the applicant's house along with the muhtar, Yusuf Özkum, Mehmet Özdamar and the brother-in-law of the deceased.
Refik Öztümen and those with him looked for a clue that could have shed light on the incident but could not find anything.
Refik Öztümen and those with him did not consider taking fingerprints on account of the fact that the incident had taken place outside the house.

The officers assigned by Refik Öztümen visited the families living in the close vicinity and further away from the scene of the incident and noted their names, interviewing those who were at home at the time of the incident.
The officers also went to the home of the Khan family of Pakistani origin and established that the family was not at home.
Refik Öztümen rang the bell of the Khan family the next day and the following evening but to no avail.
The police officers guarded the applicant's house until she arrived from abroad.

Apart from the cartridges found at the scene of the incident, the applicant and the officers in charge conducted a search along the whole street with a view to finding anything that might have been left by the assailants, but could not find anything.

The cartridges found at the scene of Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing were first examined against those in the "TRNC" and no matches could be found, then they were sent to a forensic laboratory in Ankara, but no positive result had been obtained about the weapon which could have discharged them.
The weapon found in the possession of Abdullah Çatlı following his death was also put through a forensic test in connection with the killing of Mr Kutlu Adalı, and the result was negative.
Refik Öztümen rejected the applicant's allegation that he had told her sister-in-law that the security forces had given him instructions not to follow the investigation effectively.
Refik Öztümen stressed that the applicant had never asked him to take statements from Mr Ziya Kasapoğlu.
Refik Öztümen led the investigation carried out in October 2002.
In view of the allegations that the Turkish armed forces had been involved in the killing of Mr Kutlu Adalı, Hasan Peker Günal asked the General Police Headquarters to brief him about the event.

At the end of August or early September 1996, Mr Atilla Sav and his delegation briefed Hasan Peker Günal about the killing of Mr Kutlu Adalı and the current state of the investigation at the office of the Chief of Police.

According to the Constitution of the "TRNC", the police were under the authority of the commander of the security forces in the administrative field, and in the judicial field operated under the supervision of the chief prosecutor's office.
The applicant wrote a letter to Hasan Peker Günal complaining about the conduct of the investigation into her husband's killing.
Hasan Peker Günal told the applicant through the police liaison officer that he was unable to intervene in a judicial affair but, if she wished, he could meet her.

A meeting was held on 12 December 1996 at the office of the chief of police, Mr Atilla Sav, attended by Mr Atilla Sav, the applicant, her daughter, Hasan Peker Günal and a few other police officers who were involved in the investigation.
During the meeting on 12 December 1996, the applicant was given all relevant information about the investigation into her husband's killing.

Hasan Peker Günal asked the investigators to take all necessary measures to find the perpetrators of the murder so that they could save the honour of the "TRNC" and that of the security forces whose involvement in the event was in question.
Hasan Peker Günal was informed about developments in the investigation into Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing in the course of monthly coordination meetings.

Hasan Peker Günal told the police force to examine even the slightest suspicion and made it clear that if they wanted to investigate anything connected with the armed forces or any members of the armed forces he would not obstruct it.
There was not the slightest indication of any member of the security forces being involved in the killing of Mr Kutlu Adalı.
Atilla Sav was regularly informed by the officers about developments in the investigation into Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing.
On 12 December 1996 a meeting was held in Atilla Sav's office with the applicant, her daughter, Hasan Peker Günal and Mehmet Özdamar, who was then the chief of the forensic police.
The meeting on 12 December 1996 was held at the request of the applicant.

At the meeting on 12 December 1996, the applicant gave all relevant information to the participants about the incident and complained that she had been receiving anonymous phone calls during which she had been threatened.
At the meeting on 12 December 1996, the applicant was advised to apply to the telecommunications department to have her line monitored.
At the meeting on 12 December 1996, the applicant raised her suspicion about Mr Hüseyin Demirci and was told that statements from Mr Demirci had been taken by the police.
Atilla Sav did not need to intervene in the investigation in any way since there were no deficiencies and it was being conducted according to its normal course.
When the police had completed the investigation, the files had been given to the chief prosecutor who had supervised the investigation.
Galip Mendi noted that he had not been involved in the investigation into Mr Kutlu Adalı's killing and that the oral evidence hearing was the first time he had been questioned about it.

Galip Mendi was aware of the allegations that the Civil Defence Organisation had been involved in the killing of Mr Kutlu Adalı, but stated that neither he nor the Civil Defence Organisation had a problem with Mr Adalı.
Galip Mendi did not deem it necessary to carry out an investigation within the Civil Defence Organisation as he considered that the allegations were totally unfounded.
